pos: adj. (belonging exclusively to one owner; a private possession — not, as in modern usage, strange)
etymology: Latin peculium, private property, from pecus, cattle — a man's own herd, as distinct from the common stock. The Authorized Version never uses the word to mean odd; it always means belonging exclusively to.
biblical_def: “If ye will obey my voice indeed, and keep my covenant, then ye shall be a peculiar treasure unto me above all people: for all the earth is mine” (Exo 19:5). The clause at the end is the point. All the earth belongs to God by creation; Israel belongs to Him as a man's private treasure belongs to him — his own, set apart from the general holding. Deuteronomy repeats it twice: “the LORD hath chosen thee to be a peculiar people unto himself, above all the nations that are upon the earth” (Deu 14:2), and the LORD “hath avouched thee this day to be his peculiar people” (Deu 26:18). The psalmist puts it beyond doubt: “the LORD hath chosen Jacob unto himself, and Israel for his peculiar treasure” (Psa 135:4). And the New Testament transfers the whole title to the church without hesitation: “ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people” (1Pe 2:9), and Paul says why — Christ “gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works” (Tit 2:14). Purchase is the ground of ownership. What makes a people peculiar is not their manners but a price paid for them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines peculiar as appropriate, belonging to a person and to no other; and notes that the sense of odd or singular is a secondary and later use.
webster_full: PECULIAR, a. Appropriate; belonging to a person and not to others.
1. Particular; special. My case is peculiar.
2. Singular; unusual.
3. Belonging to a nation, system or other thing, and distinguishing it from others.
PECULIUM, n. The private property of a person; that which is exclusively his own.
scriptures: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Exo 19:5
Now therefore, if ye will obey my voice indeed, and keep my covenant, then ye shall be a peculiar treasure unto me above all people: for all the earth is mine:
Tit 2:14
Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.
For the LORD hath chosen Jacob unto himself, and Israel for his peculiar treasure.
corruption_summary: “A peculiar people” is read as a licence for eccentricity; it means a purchased possession, and the oddity Scripture requires is holiness.
corruption_paragraphs: Because the English word has drifted to mean strange, 1 Peter 2:9 has been made a warrant for cultivated oddity — distinctiveness by mannerism, vocabulary and cultural refusal, as though the church's calling were to be noticeably unusual. The Greek is a people for a possession, and Titus 2:14 gives the mechanism: Christ gave Himself to purchase them. The distinctiveness that follows is moral, not stylistic — zealous of good works, that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness. A church odd in its habits and ordinary in its holiness has got the adjective and missed the noun.

The second thing to hold is the transfer. Every phrase Peter uses in 2:9 was spoken to Israel at Sinai — chosen, royal priesthood, holy nation, peculiar treasure — and he applies it without qualification to a scattered mixed congregation of Jewish and Gentile believers in Asia Minor. That is the whole doctrine of the church as the true Israel of God, grafted into the same olive tree, heirs of the same promises through Christ. Replacement is the wrong word for it; it is inclusion into the covenant people by the Seed to whom the promises were made.
roots_summary: Hebrew segullah (H5459), a peculiar treasure, a private possession; Greek laos eis peripoiesin (G2992, G4047), a people for a possession; periousios (G4041), one's own.
roots_lines: Hebrew segullah (H5459) — a treasured private possession, a king's personal wealth as distinct from the state's; Exodus 19:5, Deuteronomy 14:2, 26:18, Psalm 135:4, Malachi 3:17.
Greek periousios (G4041) — one's own, of a special possession; Titus 2:14, the Septuagint's word for segullah.
Greek peripoiesis (G4047) — an acquisition, a purchased possession; 1 Peter 2:9, Ephesians 1:14.
Greek lutroo (G3084) — to redeem by paying a ransom; Titus 2:14, that he might redeem us from all iniquity.
Greek zelotes (G2207) — zealous, an enthusiast; the mark of the purchased people — zealous of good works.
usage: “A peculiar treasure unto me above all people: for all the earth is mine”.
“An holy nation, a peculiar people” — every phrase spoken first at Sinai.
“Purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works”.

pos: v. (belonged to; was the property or concern of)
etymology: Latin pertinere, to reach through, to belong. In the Authorized Version pertained is the language of title: it marks what was legally somebody's, and the narratives in which it appears are usually about property changing hands justly or unjustly.
biblical_def: This is a word of ownership, and the stories it appears in are about who has a right to what. The angel of the LORD “sat under an oak which was in Ophrah, that pertained unto Joash the Abiezrite” while Gideon threshed wheat by the winepress to hide it from the Midianites (Jdg 6:11) — a man on his own family's land, hiding his own grain, because the land no longer functioned as his. David's complaint about Nabal is a claim of stewardship: “in vain have I kept all that this fellow hath in the wilderness, so that nothing was missed of all that pertained unto him: and he hath requited me evil for good” (1Sa 25:21). And the word carries the two halves of the Mephibosheth story, which turn on it exactly. First, kindness: “I have given unto thy master's son all that pertained to Saul and to all his house” (2Sa 9:9). Then, on the day David fled from Absalom and Ziba met him with provisions and a slander, injustice: “Behold, thine are all that pertained unto Mephibosheth” (2Sa 16:4). A lame man's whole estate was transferred on one servant's unexamined word, from a king in a hurry. When David returns, Mephibosheth answers for himself, and David divides the land — a judgment that satisfies nobody and is quietly one of the saddest verses in the book.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pertain as to belong, to be the property, right or duty of; and to have relation to, to concern.
webster_full: PERTAIN, v.i. To belong; to be the property, right or duty of.
1. To have relation to; to concern; as, the things which pertain to the kingdom of God.
PERTAINING, ppr. Belonging; concerning.
APPERTAIN, v.i. To belong, whether by right, nature or appointment.
scriptures: Then said the king to Ziba, Behold, thine are all that pertained unto Mephibosheth. And Ziba said, I humbly beseech thee that I may find grace in thy sight, my lord, O king.
Then the king called to Ziba, Saul's servant, and said unto him, I have given unto thy master's son all that pertained to Saul and to all his house.
Jdg 6:11

And there came an angel of the LORD, and sat under an oak which was in Ophrah, that pertained unto Joash the Abiezrite: and his son Gideon threshed wheat by the winepress, to hide it from the Midianites.
Now David had said, Surely in vain have I kept all that this fellow hath in the wilderness, so that nothing was missed of all that pertained unto him: and he hath requited me evil for good.
corruption_summary: Judgment is passed on one side's account; David gave away a man's estate on a servant's report without hearing him.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Samuel 16:4 is a case study in a sin the law of God specifically legislates against. Ziba arrived at the right moment with donkeys, bread, raisins and wine, and a story about his master; and David, exhausted, fleeing, and grateful, gave him everything Mephibosheth owned in a single sentence, without hearing the other party. Deuteronomy requires two or three witnesses and the hearing of both sides; Proverbs 18:17 states the principle exactly: he that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him. The generous benefactor of chapter 9 became the hasty judge of chapter 16, and the difference was that in the second case he was tired, frightened and being fed.

The principle to recover is that the timing and manner of a report are part of the evidence. Slander arrives helpfully, at a moment of need, from someone who has done you a kindness, and it asks for a decision now. Church courts, elderships and families are wrecked by this pattern more often than by open malice. The remedy is procedural and unglamorous: hear both, take witnesses, and refuse to decide a man's case in his absence, however credible the man in front of you appears.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'asher le-, that which is to (belonging to); nachalah (H5159), an inheritance; sadeh (H7704), a field.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'asher le- — the possessive construction, literally which is to; rendered pertained unto throughout the historical books.
Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — inheritance, possession; the land that pertained to a family by tribal allotment and could not simply be sold away.
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — covenant kindness, mercy; 2 Samuel 9:1, David's question — that I may shew him kindness for Jonathan's sake.
Hebrew gath (H1660) — a winepress; where Gideon threshed wheat, because the threshingfloor was too exposed.
Hebrew 'ed (H5707) — a witness; the office Deuteronomy 19:15 requires before any matter is established.
usage: “Thine are all that pertained unto Mephibosheth” — decided without hearing him.
“All that pertained to Saul and to all his house” — the kindness of chapter nine.
“Nothing was missed of all that pertained unto him” — David's claim against Nabal.

pos: adj. (the ordinal of fifty — in the law, the year of jubile)
etymology: From fifty, Saxon fiftig. Its two great occurrences are in one law: after seven sabbaths of years, forty and nine years, the fiftieth year is hallowed and liberty is proclaimed.
biblical_def: “And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you; and ye shall return every man unto his possession, and ye shall return every man unto his family” (Lev 25:10). Every fiftieth year: debts released, Hebrew servants freed, land returned to the family that had lost it. Two returns are commanded — to a possession and to a family — and the second is not decoration; the law is as concerned with households reconstituted as with acres restored. “A jubile shall that fiftieth year be unto you: ye shall not sow, neither reap that which groweth of itself in it, nor gather the grapes in it of thy vine undressed” (Lev 25:11) — following the forty-ninth, which was itself a sabbath year, so that Israel was asked to trust God for two harvests they had not planted. The kings' chronicles use the ordinal in the ordinary way to date reigns: Pekahiah began to reign “in the fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah” (2Ki 15:23). Our Lord opened His ministry by reading Isaiah 61 in the synagogue at Nazareth — to preach deliverance to the captives… to preach the acceptable year of the LORD — and sat down and said, This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears. The jubilee trumpet was a shadow; He is the liberty.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives fiftieth as the ordinal of fifty; and jubilee as, among the Israelites, every fiftieth year, being the year following the revolution of seven weeks of years, at which time all slaves were liberated and lands returned to their former owners.
webster_full: FIFTIETH, a. The ordinal of fifty; as the fiftieth part of a foot.

JUBILEE, n. Among the Israelites, every fiftieth year, being the year following the revolution of seven weeks of years, at which time all the slaves were liberated, and all lands which had been alienated during the whole period reverted to their former owners.
1. A season of great public joy and festivity.
LIBERTY, n. Freedom from restraint; the power of acting as one thinks fit.
scriptures: And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you; and ye shall return every man unto his possession, and ye shall return every man unto his family.
A jubile shall that fiftieth year be unto you: ye shall not sow, neither reap that which groweth of itself in it, nor gather the grapes in it of thy vine undressed.
In the fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah Pekahiah the son of Menahem began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and reigned two years.
corruption_summary: The jubilee is enlisted as a programme of economic redistribution; Leviticus makes it the restoration of families to their own inheritance under a divine title.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 25 is regularly conscripted for modern redistributive politics, and the fit is poor in both directions. The jubilee does not abolish property; it protects it, by returning each family to its own inheritance and preventing the permanent accumulation of land in a few hands. Nothing is transferred to the state, no central authority administers it, and the restoration is to a household rather than to a class. Equally, the chapter refuses the absolutist reading of ownership: the land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me. Human title is real and derived, and the jubilee is the yearly reminder of whose it is.

What must not be lost in the argument is the gospel shape of the year. Debt cancelled, bondmen freed, the exile restored to his family, and a trumpet on the day of atonement to start it — liberty proclaimed on the very day the blood was carried into the holiest. Our Lord read the jubilee text at Nazareth and applied it to Himself. The believer's release from a debt he could never repay, and his restoration to a family and an inheritance, is the substance of which the fiftieth year was the shadow.
roots_summary: Hebrew yobel (H3104), the jubile — a ram's horn, and the year it announced; deror (H1865), liberty, release; 'achuzzah (H272), a possession.
roots_lines: Hebrew yobel (H3104) — a ram's horn, and by extension the year proclaimed by it; Leviticus 25:10-13.
Hebrew deror (H1865) — liberty, a free running; Leviticus 25:10, Isaiah 61:1, Jeremiah 34:8 — the word inscribed on the Liberty Bell.
Hebrew 'achuzzah (H272) — a possession, a holding; what every man returned to.
Hebrew mishpachah (H4940) — a family, a clan; the second return the law commands.
Greek eniauton kuriou dekton — the acceptable year of the Lord; Luke 4:19, read by our Lord at Nazareth.
usage: “Ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty”.
“Return every man unto his possession… every man unto his family” — two returns.
“Ye shall not sow, neither reap” — the second unplanted year in a row.

pos: adj. (the ordinal of forty — the year the wilderness generation ended)
etymology: From forty, Saxon feowertig. Forty is Scripture's number of testing and of a completed probation, and the fortieth year is the year the wilderness wandering came to its end.
biblical_def: “Aaron the priest went up into mount Hor at the commandment of the LORD, and died there, in the fortieth year after the children of Israel were come out of the land of Egypt, in the first day of the fifth month” (Num 33:38). The high priest who had made the golden calf, borne the names of the tribes on his breastplate for forty years, and been forbidden the land with Moses at Meribah, climbed a mountain at God's commandment, was stripped of his garments, and died. The Aaronic priesthood is announced from the beginning as a priesthood that dies — the argument Hebrews builds on, that they were many priests because they were not suffered to continue by reason of death. In the same year Moses begins his last sermon: “it came to pass in the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, on the first day of the month, that Moses spake unto the children of Israel, according unto all that the LORD had given him in commandment” (Deu 1:3) — the whole book of Deuteronomy delivered in the final weeks of a life, to a generation that had been children when the spies returned. Chronicles dates a Levitical search “in the fortieth year of the reign of David” (1Ch 26:31), and Asa “died in the one and fortieth year of his reign” (2Ch 16:13) — diseased in his feet and seeking to the physicians and not to the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives fortieth as the ordinal of forty, the fourth tenth; and forty as four times ten, a number frequent in Scripture for periods of trial.
webster_full: FORTIETH, a. The fourth tenth; noting the number next after the thirty-ninth.
FORTY, a. Four times ten.
WILDERNESS, n. A desert; a tract of land or region uncultivated and uninhabited by human beings.
PROBATION, n. Trial; examination; proof; any proceeding designed to ascertain truth or fitness.
scriptures: And Aaron the priest went up into mount Hor at the commandment of the LORD, and died there, in the fortieth year after the children of Israel were come out of the land of Egypt, in the first day of the fifth month.
Deu 1:3

And it came to pass in the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, on the first day of the month, that Moses spake unto the children of Israel, according unto all that the LORD had given him in commandment unto them;

Among the Hebronites was Jerijah the chief, even among the Hebronites, according to the generations of his fathers. In the fortieth year of the reign of David they were sought for, and there were found among them mighty men of valour at Jazer of Gilead.
And Asa slept with his fathers, and died in the one and fortieth year of his reign.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The ordinal is plain; what a modern reader loses is the weight Scripture gives to the number forty as a completed period of testing — the flood, the wandering, Moses on the mount, Elijah to Horeb, our Lord in the wilderness.

The principle to recover is that a probation ends. The fortieth year came, and with it the death of Aaron on a mountain and the last sermon of Moses to a generation who had been children when their fathers refused to go up. God is patient through long testing and the testing has a term. That cuts two ways for a reader: it is a comfort, because no wilderness in a believer's life is open-ended, and it is a warning, because a season of God's forbearance is not indefinite. Asa is the sharper instance — a good king who finished badly, diseased in his feet in his thirty-ninth year, seeking to the physicians and not to the LORD, and dead in his forty-first. Forty years of reformation did not guarantee the last two.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'arba'im (H705), forty; midbar (H4057), wilderness; Hor (H2023), the mountain where Aaron died.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'arba'im (H705) — forty; the number of the flood's rain, the wandering, Moses on Sinai, Elijah to Horeb, and our Lord's temptation.
Hebrew Hor (H2023) — Mount Hor, on the edge of Edom, where Aaron was stripped of his garments and died.
Hebrew midbar (H4057) — wilderness, the place of testing; where a generation fell and a generation was formed.
Hebrew Meribah (H4809) — strife; the water where Moses and Aaron forfeited the land.
Greek tessarakonta (G5062) — forty; Matthew 4:2, Acts 1:3, Hebrews 3:9-17.
usage: “Died there, in the fortieth year” — a priesthood that dies.
“In the fortieth year… Moses spake unto the children of Israel”.
“Died in the one and fortieth year of his reign” — Asa, seeking to the physicians.

pos: v. (the older past participle of lie: lain)
etymology: An archaic past participle of the verb to lie, standing where modern English writes lain. It is a form, not a different word, and mistaking it for the legal lien (a claim on property) is a common modern error.
biblical_def: The form appears three times. Abimelech rebukes Isaac for calling Rebekah his sister: “What is this thou hast done unto us? one of the people might lightly have lien with thy wife, and thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us” (Gen 26:10). A pagan king lectures a patriarch on the guilt his deception would have brought upon a whole nation — the second generation to try that lie, and the second time a heathen ruler had to correct it. Jeremiah uses the form in his indictment of Judah's idolatry: “Lift up thine eyes unto the high places, and see where thou hast not been lien with. In the ways hast thou sat for them, as the Arabian in the wilderness; and thou hast polluted the land with thy whoredoms” (Jer 3:2) — spiritual adultery described in the plainest possible terms, because the prophets refuse to make idolatry sound respectable. And the third is one of the strangest and loveliest verses in the psalter: “Though ye have lien among the pots, yet shall ye be as the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her feathers with yellow gold” (Psa 68:13). Whatever the pots exactly were — sheepfolds, cooking hearths, the ash-heaps of a camp — the sense is clear: a people who have lain in the soot are promised the plumage of a dove in silver and gold.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives lien as the participle of lie, now written lain; and notes the distinct legal noun lien, a claim upon property, as an unrelated word.
webster_full: LIEN, participle of lie. Lain. [Obsolete or antiquated.]
LIE, v.i. To be in a horizontal position, or nearly so; to rest on any thing lengthwise.
LIEN, n. In law, a legal claim; the right of holding the property of another as security for a debt.
POT, n. A vessel more deep than broad, used for holding liquors and for other purposes.
scriptures: Though ye have lien among the pots, yet shall ye be as the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her feathers with yellow gold.
And Abimelech said, What is this thou hast done unto us? one of the people might lightly have lien with thy wife, and thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us.
Jer 3:2

Lift up thine eyes unto the high places, and see where thou hast not been lien with. In the ways hast thou sat for them, as the Arabian in the wilderness; and thou hast polluted the land with thy whoredoms and with thy wickedness.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is an archaic verb form, and the only hazard is confusing it with the unrelated legal noun.

The principle to recover is the promise of Psalm 68:13, which is the pattern of the whole gospel. Though ye have lien among the pots — blackened, among the ashes, in the place of drudgery — yet shall ye be as the wings of a dove covered with silver. Scripture does not deny where a man has lain; it names it plainly, as Jeremiah 3:2 names Judah's. And it sets against that a transformation the man cannot perform on himself and would not have imagined. Such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus. The soot is real, and so is the silver.
roots_summary: Hebrew shakab (H7901), to lie down; shephattayim (H8240), the sheepfolds or hearths rendered pots; yonah (H3123), a dove.
roots_lines: Hebrew shakab (H7901) — to lie down, to lie with; Genesis 26:10, Psalm 68:13, Jeremiah 3:2.
Hebrew shephattayim (H8240) — a dual noun of uncertain meaning: sheepfolds, hearths, or the two rows of stones a pot rests on; Psalm 68:13, Judges 5:16 (the sheepfolds).
Hebrew yonah (H3123) — a dove; the image of the transformed people, and the sign at our Lord's baptism.
Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to commit whoredom; the standing prophetic verb for idolatry.
Hebrew 'asham (H817) — guilt, a trespass offering; Genesis 26:10, thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us.
usage: “Though ye have lien among the pots” — and then the silver and the gold.
“One of the people might lightly have lien with thy wife” — a pagan rebuking a patriarch.
“See where thou hast not been lien with” — the prophets do not soften idolatry.

pos: v. (proved true; made good by the event)
etymology: Latin verus, true, and facere, to make — to make good, to show true. In the Authorized Version the word is used of words being proved by what happens, and twice it is the prayer that God's own word may be made good.
biblical_def: Joseph, unrecognized, sets his brothers a test: “bring your youngest brother unto me; so shall your words be verified, and ye shall not die. And they did so” (Gen 42:20). Their claim to be honest men would be proved not by protestation but by producing Benjamin — that is, by whether they would treat Rachel's other son as they had treated the first. Words are verified by events, and the whole of Genesis 42-45 is the working out of that single test, ending with Judah offering himself in the boy's place. The other two occurrences are the same sentence, prayed at the dedication of the temple: “And now, O God of Israel, let thy word, I pray thee, be verified, which thou spakest unto thy servant David my father” (1Ki 8:26; 2Ch 6:17). Solomon has just built the house and has nothing to plead but a promise. That is the settled posture of biblical prayer — not asking God for something He has not said, but asking Him to make good what He has said. Every great prayer in Scripture does this: Moses at Sinai pleading the oath to Abraham, Daniel in Babylon reading the seventy years in Jeremiah and then praying them, our Lord teaching us to pray thy kingdom come.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines verify as to prove to be true, to confirm; and to fulfil, as a promise — citing the prayer that God's word may be verified.
webster_full: VERIFY, v.t. To prove to be true; to confirm.
1. To fulfil, as a promise; to confirm the truth of a prediction; to show to be true.
VERIFIED, pp. Proved; confirmed; fulfilled.
VERITY, n. Truth; consonance of a statement, proposition or other thing to fact.
scriptures: And now, O God of Israel, let thy word, I pray thee, be verified, which thou spakest unto thy servant David my father.
But bring your youngest brother unto me; so shall your words be verified, and ye shall not die. And they did so.
Now then, O LORD God of Israel, let thy word be verified, which thou hast spoken unto thy servant David.
corruption_summary: Prayer is treated as the presentation of wishes; Solomon prays God's own promise back to Him and asks for nothing else.
corruption_paragraphs: Most instruction on prayer begins with what the pray-er wants and how to ask for it. Solomon at the dedication of the temple — the longest recorded prayer of any Old Testament king, at the high point of Israel's history — asks for one thing: let thy word be verified, which thou spakest unto thy servant David. He is not informing God of a need or negotiating for a favour; he is holding up a promise and asking that it be made good. That is what the Puritans meant by pleading the promises, and it is the difference between prayer that is finally about the one praying and prayer that is finally about God's faithfulness to His own word.

The Genesis use adds the other half. Joseph tells his brothers their words will be verified by an action, not by an assurance, and the verification takes three chapters, a famine, a silver cup and Judah's offer to become a bondman in Benjamin's place. Scripture applies the same standard to professions of faith: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works. Words are verified by what a man does when the test arrives, and the test is usually the same situation that exposed him the first time.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'aman (H539), to confirm, to be established, to be faithful — the root of amen; dabar (H1697), word; bachan (H974), to test, to try.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'aman (H539) — to confirm, to support, to be faithful or established; 1 Kings 8:26, 2 Chronicles 6:17 — and the root of amen and of faith.
Hebrew bachan (H974) — to examine, to prove, to try as metal; Genesis 42:20, so shall your words be proved.
Hebrew dabar (H1697) — word, promise, matter; the thing Solomon asks to be verified.
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — covenant faithfulness; the ground on which any promise is pleaded.
Greek bebaioo (G950) — to confirm, to make firm; 2 Corinthians 1:20, all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen.
usage: “Let thy word, I pray thee, be verified” — the whole of Solomon's request.
“So shall your words be verified” — and it took three chapters.
“Let thy word be verified, which thou hast spoken unto thy servant David”.

pos: v. (past tense of withdraw: drew back, retired, took away)
etymology: From with in its old sense of back, and draw. Scripture uses the verb for three very different retreats: God withholding His hand, our Lord retiring to pray, and Peter drawing back from a table for fear of men.
biblical_def: Our Lord withdrew habitually, and Luke names the reason: “he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed” (Luk 5:16) — the sentence comes immediately after the fame of His healing spread abroad and great multitudes came together. The busier the ministry, the more deliberate the withdrawal. Matthew records another kind: when the Pharisees held a council to destroy Him, “he withdrew himself from thence: and great multitudes followed him, and he healed them all” (Mat 12:15). He avoided the confrontation until the hour appointed, and did not stop healing while He avoided it. Mark records a withdrawal to the sea with His disciples (Mar 3:7). Against these stands the withdrawal Paul withstood to the face: “before that certain came from James, he did eat with the Gentiles: but when they were come, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision” (Gal 2:12). Peter did not preach error; he moved to another table, and Paul says the gospel itself was at stake, because a table divided by circumcision denies justification by faith alone in practice while confessing it in words. Ezekiel gives God's own withdrawal in mercy: “Nevertheless I withdrew mine hand, and wrought for my name's sake” (Eze 20:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines withdraw as to take back, to recall, to take from; and intransitively, to retire, to retreat, to quit a company or place.
webster_full: WITHDRAW, v.t. To take back; to take from.
1. To recall; to cause to leave; as, to withdraw a man from an employment.
WITHDRAW, v.i. To retire; to retreat; to quit a company or place.
WITHDREW, pret. of withdraw.
scriptures: Luk 5:16
And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed.
Gal 2:12
For before that certain came from James, he did eat with the Gentiles: but when they were come, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision.
But when Jesus knew it, he withdrew himself from thence: and great multitudes followed him, and he healed them all;
Nevertheless I withdrew mine hand, and wrought for my name's sake, that it should not be polluted in the sight of the heathen, in whose sight I brought them forth.
corruption_summary: Table fellowship is treated as a matter of preference; Paul calls Peter's withdrawal a departure from the truth of the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 2:12 is the most instructive church-discipline case in the New Testament, and it is instructive precisely because Peter's sin looks so small. He did not teach that circumcision was necessary; he moved seats. Paul's verdict is that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel and that he withstood him to the face before them all, because a table segregated by law-keeping preaches justification by works no matter what the pulpit says. What a church does with its fellowship is doctrine in practice, and practice that contradicts confession will be believed over confession every time.

The other lesson is our Lord's withdrawing, which the modern minister most needs. Luke 5:15-16 is one sentence of expanding fame followed by one sentence of retreat: so much the more went there a fame abroad of him… And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed. The withdrawal was habitual and it was for prayer, not for rest merely. A ministry that grows without a corresponding growth in withdrawal will be run on the fumes of its own reputation. The Son of God, who had no sin to confess and perfect communion with the Father, still went into the wilderness alone; there is no one for whom this is optional.
roots_summary: Greek anachoreo (G402), to withdraw, to retire; hupostello (G5288), to draw back, to shrink from; Hebrew shub (H7725), to turn back.
roots_lines: Greek anachoreo (G402) — to go back, to withdraw, to retire; Matthew 12:15, Mark 3:7 — the root behind anchorite.
Greek hupochoreo (G5298) — to withdraw, to retire; Luke 5:16, 9:10.
Greek hupostello (G5288) — to draw back, to shrink from through fear; Galatians 2:12, and Hebrews 10:38, if any man draw back.
Greek aphorizo (G873) — to separate, to set off by a boundary; Galatians 2:12, he withdrew and separated himself.
Hebrew shub (H7725) — to turn back, to withdraw; Ezekiel 20:22, I withdrew mine hand.
usage: “He withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed” — after the fame spread.
“He withdrew and separated himself, fearing them” — and Paul withstood him.
“I withdrew mine hand, and wrought for my name's sake”.

pos: v. (to separate, to divide, to set apart from)
etymology: Latin separare, to separate, through Old French sevrer. In Scripture God is nearly always the one who severs, and He does it twice in Exodus to distinguish His people in the middle of a judgment.
biblical_def: In the plagues God twice announces a severing. “I will sever in that day the land of Goshen, in which my people dwell, that no swarms of flies shall be there; to the end thou mayest know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth” (Exo 8:22). And of the murrain: “the LORD shall sever between the cattle of Israel and the cattle of Egypt: and there shall nothing die of all that is the children's of Israel” (Exo 9:4). The stated purpose is revelation — to the end thou mayest know. The severing is not merely protective; it is evidential, a line drawn through a country so that everyone can see there is a God who distinguishes. The final severing is our Lord's, at the end of the parable of the net: “So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just” (Mat 13:49). Note the direction — the wicked are severed from among the just, which assumes they were mixed together until then, exactly as the tares grew with the wheat and the bad fish came up in the same net. The separation is at the end, it is performed by angels and not by men, and it is final. Ezekiel adds a grim administrative use: men “of continual employment” severed out to bury the dead of Gog's army and cleanse the land (Eze 39:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sever as to part or divide by violence, to separate by parting or rending; and to separate one thing from another, to disjoin.
webster_full: SEVER, v.t. To part or divide by violence; to separate by parting or rending; as, to sever the body or the arm at a single stroke.
1. To part from the rest by violence; as, to sever the head from the body.
2. To separate and put in a different order or place; as, the angels shall sever the wicked from among the just.
3. To disjoin; to disunite; in a general sense, but usually implying violence.
scriptures: So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just,
Exo 8:22
And I will sever in that day the land of Goshen, in which my people dwell, that no swarms of flies shall be there; to the end thou mayest know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth.
Exo 9:4
And the LORD shall sever between the cattle of Israel and the cattle of Egypt: and there shall nothing die of all that is the children's of Israel.
And they shall sever out men of continual employment, passing through the land to bury with the passengers those that remain upon the face of the earth, to cleanse it:
corruption_summary: The final separation is denied or brought forward; Scripture says the angels do it, at the end, out of a mixed field.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors run opposite ways from Matthew 13:49. The first denies the severing altogether, insisting that a God of love makes no final division — against which our Lord's own parables of the tares, the net and the sheep and the goats stand immovable, all of them ending in a separation He performs. The second brings the severing forward and gives it to men: the sect that believes it can produce a pure church now by sufficiently rigorous exclusion. The parable of the tares forbids it explicitly — let both grow together until the harvest — not because purity does not matter but because we cannot tell the plants apart without uprooting wheat.

This is not an argument against church discipline, which the same Lord commands in Matthew 18 and Paul enforces in 1 Corinthians 5. Discipline deals with open, unrepented sin in a professing member and aims at his restoration; it never claims to be the final judgment. The distinction is the whole of a healthy ecclesiology: the church judges what is visible and leaves the heart to the One who reads it, knowing that the angels will do at the end of the world what no eldership can do now.
roots_summary: Hebrew palah (H6395), to distinguish, to set apart; badal (H914), to divide, to separate; Greek aphorizo (G873), to mark off by a boundary.
roots_lines: Hebrew palah (H6395) — to distinguish, to make a distinction, to set apart; Exodus 8:22, 9:4, 11:7, 33:16.
Hebrew badal (H914) — to divide, to separate; Genesis 1:4 (light from darkness), Leviticus 20:24-26 (Israel from the nations).
Greek aphorizo (G873) — to separate, to mark off by boundaries; Matthew 13:49, 25:32, of the sheep from the goats.
Greek sunteleia tou aionos (G4930, G165) — the end of the age or world; the appointed time of the severing.
Greek zizanion (G2215) — tares; the parable that forbids an early separation by human hands.
usage: “The angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just”.
“I will sever in that day the land of Goshen” — that thou mayest know.
“The LORD shall sever between the cattle of Israel and the cattle of Egypt”.

pos: adv. (within; in the inner man — as distinguished from what is shown)
etymology: From inward, Saxon innaweard. The adverb marks the gap between what a man is and what he displays, and all three occurrences turn on that gap — twice as hypocrisy, once as the true circumcision.
biblical_def: “Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves” (Mat 7:15). The clothing is not a disguise that is easily seen through; it is sheep's clothing, and the sheep are supposed to be fooled. Our Lord's test in the following verses is not doctrinal cross-examination but fruit, examined over time: ye shall know them by their fruits — and the fruit He goes on to describe is not results but the doing of the Father's will. Psalm 62 gives the domestic version: “they bless with their mouth, but they curse inwardly” (Psa 62:4). And Romans supplies the positive: “he is a Jew, which is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter; whose praise is not of men, but of God” (Rom 2:29). Paul has spent the chapter dismantling any claim founded on external membership, and he ends with the definition: the true Israelite is the one whose circumcision is of the heart. The Old Testament had said the same — circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart (Deu 10:16) — so this is not a New Testament innovation but the recovery of what the sign always signified. And the last clause names the reward and its audience: whose praise is not of men, but of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inwardly as in the inner parts, internally; and in the heart, privately, secretly.
webster_full: INWARDLY, adv. In the inner parts; internally.
1. In the heart; privately; secretly; as, he inwardly repines.
2. Toward the center.
INWARD, a. Internal; interior; placed or being within; as the inward structure of the body.
scriptures: Rom 2:29
But he is a Jew, which is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter; whose praise is not of men, but of God.
Mat 7:15
Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.
Psa 62:4
They only consult to cast him down from his excellency: they delight in lies: they bless with their mouth, but they curse inwardly. Selah.
corruption_summary: Inwardness is set against outward obedience as though only the heart mattered; Scripture makes the heart the source of the obedience, not its substitute.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 2:29 has been made to serve a religion of pure interiority: since what counts is the heart, the outward is dispensable — church membership optional, ordinances negotiable, public confession unnecessary, my faith is a private matter between me and God. Paul is arguing nothing of the kind. He is denying that the outward sign, held without the inward reality, avails; he is not denying the sign. The same apostle commands baptism, the Lord's table, the assembling of ourselves together and confession with the mouth. A circumcision of the heart that never reaches the hands is exactly what James calls a dead faith.

The other application is our Lord's warning, and it is directed at the church's discernment rather than at the wolves. He does not say the false prophets will be obvious; He says they will wear sheep's clothing and be inwardly ravening. Since the inside cannot be inspected directly, He gives the only test available to men: fruit, over time, measured against the will of the Father. That is slower and less satisfying than doctrinal detection, and it is what He gave us. It also means that a man's gifts, crowds and confidence prove nothing — the very next paragraph has men pleading their prophecies and mighty works and being told I never knew you.
roots_summary: Greek esothen (G2081), from within; en to krupto (G2927), in secret; Hebrew qereb (H7130), the inward part.
roots_lines: Greek esothen (G2081) — from within, inwardly; Matthew 7:15, and Matthew 23:27-28 of the whited sepulchres.
Greek en to krupto (G2927) — in the hidden place, in secret; Romans 2:29, a Jew inwardly — literally, in secret.
Greek harpax (G727) — ravening, rapacious, an extortioner; the true nature under the sheep's clothing.
Hebrew qereb (H7130) — the inward part, the midst; Psalm 62:4, they curse in their inward part.
Hebrew mul leb — to circumcise the heart; Deuteronomy 10:16, 30:6, Jeremiah 4:4 — the Old Testament root of Paul's argument.
usage: “He is a Jew, which is one inwardly” — and his praise is of God.
“Inwardly they are ravening wolves” — and the clothing is convincing.
“They bless with their mouth, but they curse inwardly”.

pos: adv. (it may be; by chance — used in Scripture where a man may not presume to state a certainty)
etymology: From per (by) and hap, chance. The word appears three times in the Authorized Version, and each occurrence marks the boundary of what a man is entitled to affirm — about God's forgiveness, about another's grief, and about providence.
biblical_def: Peter says it to Simon the sorcerer: “Repent therefore of this thy wickedness, and pray God, if perhaps the thought of thine heart may be forgiven thee” (Act 8:22). The command is unqualified — repent and pray — and the outcome is left where it belongs. Peter will not promise pardon to a man he has just told is in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity; he tells him what to do and leaves God free. That is the right way to deal with a presumptuous professor: the duty is certain, the assurance is not automatic, and mercy is real. Paul uses it pastorally in the other direction: “ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow” (2Co 2:7). The disciplined man at Corinth had repented, and Paul's fear now is that the church will keep punishing after God has forgiven. Discipline that will not end has become cruelty, and Satan gets his advantage that way as surely as by the original sin. And the loveliest use is Philemon: “For perhaps he therefore departed for a season, that thou shouldest receive him for ever” (Phm 1:15). A runaway slave's flight is read as possible providence — perhaps, because Paul will not claim to have read God's ledger, only to have noticed how it looks.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines perhaps as by chance; peradventure; it may be; and peradventure as by chance, perhaps, it may be.
webster_full: PERHAPS, adv. By chance; peradventure; it may be.
PERADVENTURE, adv. By chance; perhaps; it may be.
HAP, n. That which comes suddenly or unexpectedly; chance; fortune; accident.
PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
scriptures: Phm 1:15
For perhaps he therefore departed for a season, that thou shouldest receive him for ever;
Act 8:22
Repent therefore of this thy wickedness, and pray God, if perhaps the thought of thine heart may be forgiven thee.
So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.
corruption_summary: Providence is claimed with a confidence Scripture avoids; Paul says perhaps about a case he had every reason to be sure of.
corruption_paragraphs: Christians speak about providence with a certainty the apostles did not use. God took him for a reason, this happened so that, the Lord closed that door because — sentences that read God's secret counsel off the surface of an event. Paul, writing about a runaway slave who had been converted under his ministry and was going home to a Christian master, says perhaps he therefore departed for a season. He believed absolutely in the sovereignty of God over Onesimus' flight; he simply would not claim to know the reason. That is the exact posture Deuteronomy 29:29 requires: the secret things belong unto the LORD our God, but those things which are revealed belong unto us.

The other two uses guard the ministry at both edges. To the presumptuous man, Peter says repent and pray if perhaps — refusing to hand assurance to someone showing no evidence of grace, while refusing equally to shut the door. To a church that had disciplined a man who then repented, Paul says forgive and comfort him lest perhaps he be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. Both are the same discipline of speech: say certainly what God has said certainly, and say perhaps where He has not spoken. A ministry that reverses this — confident about providence, tentative about the gospel — has everything backwards.
roots_summary: Greek tacha (G5029), perhaps, possibly; ei ara (G1487, G686), if perhaps, if indeed; me pos (G3381), lest by any means.
roots_lines: Greek tacha (G5029) — perhaps, possibly; Philemon 15, Romans 5:7 — its only two New Testament occurrences.
Greek ei ara (G1487 with G686) — if then, if perhaps; Acts 8:22, leaving the issue with God.
Greek me pos (G3381) — lest by any means, lest perhaps; 2 Corinthians 2:7, the pastoral fear behind restoring the penitent.
Greek katapino (G2666) — to swallow up, to drink down; 2 Corinthians 2:7, swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.
Greek aionios (G166) — eternal, for ever; Philemon 15, that thou shouldest receive him for ever — the possible purpose Paul glimpses.
usage: “Perhaps he therefore departed for a season” — Paul, refusing to be certain.
“Pray God, if perhaps the thought of thine heart may be forgiven thee”.
“Lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow”.
